title: React Interview Prep — Day by Day
excerpt: A running, day-by-day set of React interview questions and answers — from JSX and components through state, props, and beyond — each with a full breakdown plus a tight, interview-ready answer to fall back on.

questions.question: What is React, and why is it used?

body.text: React is a JavaScript library (not a full framework) for building user interfaces, created by Facebook/Meta. Its core idea: build your UI as a tree of reusable components, and let React handle efficiently updating the DOM when your data changes.
Why it's used — the core problems it solves:

items: Manual DOM manipulation is slow and error-prone. Before React (and similar libraries), developers wrote imperative code like document.getElementById("x").innerHTML = ... all over the place, which becomes unmanageable as an app grows — you have to track exactly what changed and update it by hand.
React is declarative. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React figures out how to update the actual DOM to match — you don't manually touch the DOM yourself.
Component-based architecture. UI is broken into small, reusable, independent pieces (buttons, forms, cards) that manage their own logic and can be composed together.
Virtual DOM (covered in depth later) — React keeps an in-memory representation of the UI and only updates the real DOM where necessary, rather than re-rendering everything.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: React is a declarative, component-based JavaScript library for building UIs. Instead of manually manipulating the DOM step by step, you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React efficiently updates the real DOM to match — using a virtual DOM to minimize actual DOM operations. It's popular because it makes complex, interactive UIs easier to reason about and maintain through reusable, composable components.

A component is a self-contained, reusable piece of UI — it takes in data (via props) and returns what should be rendered (via JSX). Think of components as JavaScript functions that return UI instead of just a value.

items: Functional components — plain JavaScript functions (the modern standard, especially with Hooks).
Class components — ES6 classes extending React.Component (the older way).

body.text: Why components matter — composition:
Each piece is built, tested, and reasoned about independently, then assembled like building blocks. This is the fundamental unit of organization in every React app.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: A component is a reusable, self-contained building block of UI — essentially a function (or class) that accepts props as input and returns JSX describing what to render. Components let you break a complex UI into small, independent, composable pieces, which is the foundational organizing principle of any React application.

JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup directly inside JavaScript. It's not valid JavaScript on its own — it gets compiled (typically by Babel) into regular React.createElement() calls before the browser ever sees it.
Key JSX rules interviewers test:

Why use it at all instead of plain createElement calls? JSX is purely a developer-experience improvement — it lets UI structure look like the HTML it produces, which is far more readable than deeply nested createElement calls. React works identically either way; JSX is optional but nearly universal in practice.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript, which Babel compiles into React.createElement() calls before it runs. It's not required to use React, but it makes component structure far more readable than the equivalent nested function calls. Key rules: it must return a single root element, uses {} to embed JS expressions, and uses className/camelCase attributes since it's ultimately still JavaScript, not HTML.

Naming convention rule (worth knowing, it's not just style): component names must start with a capital letter (Welcome, not welcome) — this is how JSX distinguishes a custom component (<Welcome />) from a regular HTML tag (<welcome>, which React would treat as a literal, unknown HTML element).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: A functional component is just a JavaScript function that returns JSX, optionally accepting props as its parameter. It's the modern standard way to write components, especially since Hooks let functional components hold state and side effects without needing a class. The one hard rule is the name must be capitalized, since that's how JSX tells a custom component apart from a plain HTML tag.

questions.question: How do you create a class component in React?

body.text: The older way to write components — an ES6 class extending React.Component, required to implement a render() method that returns JSX.
With state (the classic pre-Hooks pattern):

Why you rarely write these today: class components require this binding gymnastics (this.state, this.props, arrow functions or manual .bind() for event handlers), and lifecycle methods (componentDidMount, etc.) are more verbose than the equivalent Hooks. Since React 16.8 introduced Hooks, functional components can do everything class components can, with less boilerplate — so new code almost always uses functional components. You'll still see class components in older/legacy codebases, which is why interviewers still ask about them.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: A class component extends React.Component and must implement a render() method returning JSX. State lives on this.state, updated via this.setState(), and props are accessed via this.props. They were the only way to have state and lifecycle methods before Hooks arrived in React 16.8. I still need to recognize them for legacy code, but new components are functional, since Hooks provide the same capabilities with less boilerplate and no this binding issues.
State is data that's local to a component and can change over time — when it changes, React automatically re-renders that component (and its children) to reflect the new value.
Key properties of state:

items: Local and private to the component that owns it — a component can't directly read or set another component's state (only pass it down as props, or lift it up).
Changing state triggers a re-render — this is the whole mechanism that makes the UI "reactive" to data changes.

Should be treated as immutable — you never mutate state directly (state.count++ ❌), you always call the updater function (setCount(count + 1) ✅), because React relies on detecting a new value to know it needs to re-render.

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: State is data a component owns internally that can change over time. When state updates via its setter function, React re-renders that component to reflect the new value. State is private to the component — you never mutate it directly, you always call the setter, since React relies on that call to know a re-render is needed.

questions.question: How does props work in React?

body.text: Props ("properties") are how a parent component passes data down to a child component — similar to function arguments, but for components.
Key properties of props:
Read-only from the child's perspective — a component receiving props can never modify them directly; only the parent that passed them can change what's sent down.

items: Flow one direction — parent → child only (this is called "unidirectional data flow" and is fundamental to how React apps are structured).
Can be anything — strings, numbers, objects, arrays, even functions (commonly used so a child can notify a parent of an event).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: Props are how data flows from a parent component into a child, similar to function parameters. They're read-only — a child can never modify the props it receives, only the parent that owns the data can change what's passed down. This one-directional flow (parent to child) is core to how React apps stay predictable, and props can carry anything, including functions, which is how children typically communicate events back up to parents.

questions.question: What is the difference between state and props?

body.text: The mental model interviewers want to hear: state is a component's own private memory. Props are input a component receives from outside — think of props like function arguments, and state like a variable declared inside the function body. A component re-renders when either changes, but only state can be changed by that component itself; props can only ever be changed by whoever owns them (the parent).

body.label: Interview-ready answer
body.text: State is data a component manages internally and can change itself via a setter — think of it as private memory. Props are data passed in from a parent, and are read-only from the receiving component's perspective — think of them like function arguments. Both trigger re-renders when they change, but a component only controls its own state; it never controls the props it receives, since those belong to whoever passed them down.
